script.opening: "Cheers for seeing me on video — I didn’t want to sit in the waiting room looking like a Simpson. So yeah, I’ve gone proper yellow, my wee’s like Coke and I feel rotten. I figured I picked up some bug travelling. I mainly need to know how long till it clears, because honestly I just need to get back to work — and is there a tablet that speeds it up?"

facts.text: If explored: prodrome of fever, nausea and aches a couple of weeks ago that he shrugged off; now jaundiced, dark urine, pale stools, RUQ ache, anorexia, profound fatigue. Ate street food and salads constantly, drank local water/ice at times. Picture fits acute viral hepatitis (A or E most likely).

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable only with a non-judgemental sexual/risk history: he had unprotected sex with a couple of new partners on the trip, and got a spur-of-the-moment tattoo in a backpacker town. He is privately terrified this is something blood-borne or sexual (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) that he’ll have to disclose to his girlfriend back home. The "how long till it clears" is partly a wish that it’s a simple tummy bug.

If reached: been with his girlfriend two years; the trip was "lads before he settles down"; the guilt is enormous and the fear of having to tell her — and of having infected her — is what’s really keeping him awake.

He is a CHEF — a food handler — and desperate to get back to work for money. Has not connected that hepatitis A/E is faeco-orally spread and that he must NOT handle food until cleared; sees the question purely as "when can I earn again."

Officially: a quick fix and a return-to-work date. Actually: to know whether this is a simple travel bug or something he caught sexually that threatens his relationship and his health — and to be tested and told honestly, without a lecture.

ice.ideas: He caught a travel tummy bug that turned his liver yellow; it’ll pass and there might be a tablet to hurry it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — unprotected sex with new partners and an unsterile tattoo abroad; private terror this is blood-borne/sexual (hep B, hep C, HIV) and that he’ll have to confess to and may have infected his girlfriend.
ice.expectations: A cure and a return-to-work date. Underneath: honest testing and answers about whether this threatens his relationship and his future health.

cues: "How long till it clears / get back to work" — fixed on a quick fix; the worry underneath isn’t voiced yet.
A pause or deflection when asked openly about the trip beyond food — the sex and tattoo waiting to be asked about safely.
"A bug travelling" stated a bit too firmly — the preferred, less-frightening explanation.

checkpoints.text: Recognises acute hepatitis from the picture and the markedly raised transaminases (ALT >1000) — most likely viral hepatitis A or E given the travel and faeco-oral exposure — and conveys that most acute viral hepatitis is self-limiting, while taking it seriously

Takes a proper exposure history non-judgementally, covering food/water AND the higher-risk routes: unprotected sex, tattoos/piercings, injections/medical/dental procedures, drug use — and so elicits the hidden blood-borne risk

Orders the right work-up: hepatitis A/B/C/E serology, HIV test (with consent), repeat LFTs + INR (synthetic function), and considers other travel causes (malaria film if any fever, lepto, etc.); explains why HIV (NICE NG60) and hepatitis B and C testing matters given his exposures, with honest windows (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020: a 4th-generation HIV test excludes infection only from 45 days after the last exposure)

Identifies the food-handler public-health duty: acute infectious hepatitis is notifiable on clinical suspicion (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010: written notice to the proper officer within 3 days, by phone if urgent); UKHSA (2024): hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, are excluded until 7 days after the onset of jaundice, with the health protection team advising on return (and on hepatitis E) — explains this clearly as protecting others, and that household and sexual contacts (including his girlfriend) need assessing for hepatitis A vaccine within 14 days of exposure

Screens for red flags of acute liver failure: any confusion/drowsiness (encephalopathy), bruising/bleeding, deepening jaundice, persistent vomiting, rising INR — and knows these mean urgent/same-day hospital assessment
Creates a safe, non-judgemental space that lets the sexual and tattoo exposure — and the relationship fear — be disclosed, rather than taking "just a travel bug" at face value

Handles the partner/disclosure anxiety with compassion and without moralising: explains testing windows honestly, that some results take time, and supports him on if/how to talk to his girlfriend and on her testing

Safety-nets and follows up clearly: alcohol/hepatotoxic-drug avoidance (incl. paracetamol caution dosing), red flags for same-day return, results/serology follow-up arranged, work-exclusion confirmed in writing, and partner-testing/sexual-health signposting

worked.txt: "You’ve got an inflamed liver — that’s what the yellow, the dark wee and the pale stools mean, and your blood test confirms it. The good news up front: most of the time, when this comes from a travel infection, it settles on its own over a few weeks. But ‘which infection’ actually matters a lot, so let’s work that out properly rather than guess."

"I ask everyone with this the same full set of questions, no judgement attached, because the cause changes the plan. Food and water abroad, yes — but also: any new sexual partners on the trip, any tattoos or piercings, any injections or procedures? … Thank you for being straight with me. That’s genuinely useful, not something to feel bad about."

"I get the sense the thing keeping you up isn’t the yellow — it’s wondering whether this is something you caught that you’d have to tell your girlfriend about. Let’s meet that head-on instead of you carrying it alone. We’ll test for the bugs that spread through food, and the ones that spread through sex and blood, so you actually KNOW rather than dread."

"Some of these show up straight away; a couple — like HIV and hepatitis C — have a window where an early test can miss them, so we may repeat them. I’m not going to pretend I can tell you today that everything’s fine. What I can promise is we find out properly, and whatever it is, there’s a plan — these are far more manageable than the 3am version in your head."

"Now the bit you didn’t expect: because the likely cause spreads through food and you’re a chef, you must not handle food or go back to the kitchen until you’re cleared — this type of hepatitis is notifiable — I’ll let the health protection team know — and the rules say at least a week off food handling from when the yellow started, with them advising when you can go back. I know that hits your income, and we’ll sort a sick note and the public-health side together. Your housemates — and your girlfriend — may also need checking or a vaccine, and that works best within two weeks of contact."

"While you recover: no alcohol at all, be careful with painkillers — I’ll tell you exactly what’s safe. If you get confused or drowsy, start bruising or bleeding, can’t keep fluids down, or go more yellow — that’s straight to hospital, don’t wait. I’ll chase your results and see you to go through them. And when you’re ready, we can think together about talking to your girlfriend and her getting tested. You’re not dealing with this on your own."

f.learning: Jaundice in a young returning traveller with ALT >1000 is acute viral hepatitis until proven otherwise — most likely A or E (faeco-oral) given the travel, and usually self-limiting. But the case is built on two things beyond the diagnosis. First, the public-health duty: he is a CHEF, hepatitis A/E is notifiable and faeco-orally spread, so he must be notified (on clinical suspicion) and excluded from food handling until 7 days after the onset of jaundice (UKHSA, 2024), with household and sexual contacts assessed for hepatitis A vaccine within 14 days of exposure. Second, the hidden agenda: a non-judgemental risk history reveals unprotected sex and an unsterile tattoo abroad and a terror of blood-borne/sexual infection (hep B, C, HIV) and of confessing to his girlfriend. Test the full panel (with HIV consent and honest windows), screen for acute liver failure red flags, give hepatotoxin/alcohol advice, and support the disclosure and partner-testing with compassion rather than a lecture. (Note: jaundice in an OLDER patient is a different animal — refers people aged 40 and over with jaundice on a suspected pancreatic cancer pathway — which does not apply to Jay at 26, and is why pinning the cause matters.)

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA Public health control and management of hepatitis A (2024) · UKHSA Green Book ch.17 (2024) · Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 · NICE NG60 · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA HIV testing guidelines (2020) · BSG abnormal liver blood tests guideline (2018)
knowledge.summary: Jaundice with ALT in the thousands in a returning traveller is acute viral hepatitis until proven otherwise, most often A or E. Check synthetic function, test the full viral and blood-borne panel with consent, notify on suspicion, and exclude a food handler from work.

points.t: Transaminases in the thousands with a modest ALP rise is a hepatocellular picture: viral, drug or toxin, ischaemic or autoimmune hepatitis. A normal INR is reassuring about synthetic function today; it must be repeated because it is the earliest marker of liver failure. BSG 2018: refer urgently if there is synthetic failure or marked derangement.

Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and core IgM, hepatitis C antibody (with RNA if positive), hepatitis E, and an HIV test with consent (NICE NG60). BSG 2018 advises HEV testing when A, B and C are negative; test it up front in a returning traveller. Malaria films if there has been any fever after travel to an endemic area.

BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020: a fourth-generation HIV test excludes infection only from 45 days after the last exposure, so an early negative needs repeating. Hepatitis C antibody can take weeks to months to appear; RNA testing detects it earlier. Tell him plainly that one clear set of results may not be the last word.

Acute infectious hepatitis is notifiable on clinical suspicion (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010): written notice to the proper officer within 3 days, by phone if urgent. UKHSA 2024: exclude hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, until 7 days after the onset of jaundice; the health protection team advises on return and on hepatitis E.

Hepatitis A is infectious from about 2 weeks before symptoms to 1 week after jaundice. UKHSA 2024: hepatitis A vaccine within 14 days of exposure for healthy close contacts aged 1 and over; the health protection team arranges it, adding immunoglobulin for higher-risk contacts. Household and sexual contacts, including his girlfriend, need assessing.

Confusion, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, a rising INR or deepening jaundice mean same-day hospital assessment. Avoid alcohol; paracetamol at standard doses only, avoiding large doses (BNF). For contrast: NICE suspected-cancer guidance refers people aged 40 and over with jaundice on a suspected pancreatic cancer pathway, which does not apply to Jay at 26.

dg.d: Open question about how he feels; heard the work and ‘quick fix’ questions without letting them set the agenda.
Chef and food handler, income worries, relationship of two years, alcohol use.
Hepatitis A, B, C and E serology; HIV with consent; repeat LFTs and INR; malaria films if febrile; repeat tests after the window period.
Hepatitis A or E vs acute hepatitis B vs drug or toxin injury; tested with food, sexual, tattoo, injecting and medication history.
Asked about confusion, drowsiness, bleeding and vomiting; normal INR noted and repeated; same-day admission criteria known.
Acute viral hepatitis, most likely A or E, explained in plain words with the cause still to confirm.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Notification on suspicion; food-handler exclusion for at least 7 days from jaundice onset per UKHSA; fit note; no alcohol, standard paracetamol doses.
Partner protection and testing, contact vaccination via the health protection team, sexual health signposting.
Liver failure red flags named; results phoned; repeat HIV and hepatitis C testing timed after the window period.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the pause about the trip and the over-firm ‘travel bug’ and opened the sexual and tattoo history safely.
Idea (food bug), concern (blood-borne infection and his girlfriend), expectation (return-to-work date and a tablet).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — unprotected sex with new partners and an unsterile tattoo abroad; private terror this is blood-borne/sexual (hep B, hep C, HIV) and that he’ll have to confess to and may have infected his girlfriend — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.

model.text: Hello Jay, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for coming on video, and I can see what you mean about the colour. Before we get to results, tell me how you’re feeling in yourself today.
model.why: Acknowledges his joke and the visible jaundice, then opens with his experience

model.text: Rotten, honestly. Yellow eyes, wee like Coke, no appetite. I reckon I caught a bug travelling. I mainly need to know how long till it clears so I can get back in the kitchen. Is there a tablet that speeds it up?

Those are fair questions and I’ll answer both. So that I give you real answers rather than guesses, can I ask about the illness and the trip first, then explain the blood test and agree a plan? Your work is definitely on the list.
model.why: Agrees an agenda that includes his work question without jumping to it

model.text: Yeah, go for it.
Take me back to when this started. What came first?
model.why: Open question to get the timeline in his words

model.text: A couple of weeks ago I had a temperature, felt sick and achy. I thought it was flu. Then four days ago the yellow started, the wee went dark and my poo went pale. Sore just under my right ribs.
Any confusion or drowsiness, bruising or bleeding from your gums, or vomiting so much you can’t keep fluids down? And has the fever come back at all?
model.why: Screens for acute liver failure and for fever that would need malaria films

model.text: No, none of that. No fever since. Just tired and off my food.
Good. Tell me about the food and water out there.
model.why: Covers the faeco-oral route for hepatitis A and E

model.text: Street food every day, salads, ice in drinks, sometimes tap water. It’s a bug from the food, right?

That’s the most likely route. Everyone I see with this gets the same full set of questions, with no judgement, because the answer changes which tests we do. On the trip, any new sexual partners, any tattoos or piercings, and any injections, medical or dental treatment?
model.why: Normalises the question and covers the blood-borne and sexual routes

model.text: …Yeah. A couple of girls, no condoms. And I got a tattoo in a hostel town. I wasn’t thinking.
Thank you for telling me. That is genuinely useful, and it isn’t something to feel ashamed about here. Any drugs by injection, and any alcohol or medicines recently, including paracetamol?
model.why: Rewards the disclosure without moralising and completes the toxin history

model.text: Never injected anything. A few beers out there, nothing since I got ill. Couple of paracetamol for the ache.
You went quiet before you told me about the trip. I wonder whether the thing keeping you awake isn’t the yellow at all.
model.why: Names the cue behind the pause and invites the hidden concern

model.text: My girlfriend. We’ve been together two years. That trip was meant to be the lads’ thing before we settle down. If this is hepatitis B or HIV, I have to tell her. And what if I’ve already given it to her?
That’s a lot to have been carrying on your own. So the real hope today is to find out whether this is a food bug or something caught through sex, and whether she’s at risk?
model.why: Reflects the concern and confirms the real expectation

model.text: Yeah. That’s it.

Here’s what I think. Your liver is inflamed, which is why you’re yellow. The pattern in your blood test, after a month of street food, most likely fits hepatitis A or E, which come from food and water. They usually settle by themselves over a few weeks, and your clotting test is normal, which tells me the liver is still doing its main jobs.
model.why: Explains acute hepatocellular hepatitis in plain words, with its likely cause

model.text: So it probably is the food?

Probably, but I won’t guess. I’d like one blood sample today that checks for hepatitis A, B, C and E, and, with your agreement, HIV. I’ll repeat the liver and clotting tests too. I should be honest that HIV and hepatitis C can take several weeks to show, so if the first results are clear we may repeat them later to be sure.
model.why: Full viral and blood-borne panel with consent, and honest testing windows

model.text: Yeah, test for all of it. I’d rather know.

Now the part you didn’t expect. Hepatitis from food spreads through food. As a chef, you mustn’t work in the kitchen until you’re cleared: at least a week from when the yellow started, and the public health team advises on your return. I have a legal duty to notify them, and they will also check whether people close to you need a vaccine.
model.why: States the food-handler exclusion and the statutory notification

model.text: A week off? I can’t afford that.

I know it hits your wages. I’ll give you a fit note, and the public health team can confirm the exclusion in writing for your employer, which also protects your job. Is money going to be a real problem?
model.why: Acknowledges the financial impact and offers practical help

model.text: I’ll manage if I get sick pay. The boss is alright.

About your girlfriend: condoms, or no sex, until your results are back. If she has been close to you since you got home, the public health team may offer her a hepatitis A vaccine, and the sexual health clinic can test her confidentially. When and how you tell her is your decision, and I’m happy to help you plan it.
model.why: Protects the partner and supports disclosure without taking control from him

model.text: Okay. I think I do need to tell her. Just not before I know what it is.

That’s a reasonable plan. While you recover: no alcohol at all, eat what you can, drink plenty, and paracetamol only at normal doses. No herbal remedies. And there isn’t a tablet to speed up this kind of hepatitis; rest is the treatment.
model.why: Hepatotoxin advice and an honest answer to his tablet question

model.text: Please go straight to A&E, or call 999 if you can’t get there, if you become confused or very sleepy, bruise or bleed easily, can’t keep fluids down, or go more yellow. I’ll ring you with the results in a few days, and we’ll book a repeat test for later.
model.why: Named acute liver failure red flags and dated follow-up

model.text: Got it.
So I know I’ve explained it properly, what will you tell your boss tomorrow?
model.why: Teach-back on the point he most needs to act on

model.text: That I’ve got hepatitis, probably from food, and I can’t cook until public health clears me. And I’ll get a sick note.
Exactly. You did the right thing by telling me everything today.
model.why: Closes warmly and reinforces the disclosure

social.t: A chef paid by the shift faces lost income from exclusion. Offer a fit note and written confirmation of exclusion from the health protection team; he is likely to be eligible for Statutory Sick Pay.
Guilt about sex outside the relationship drives both the concealment and the anxiety. Support disclosure at his pace while making sure his partner is protected and can be tested.

legal.t: Acute infectious hepatitis is notifiable on clinical suspicion under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010: written notice to the proper officer within 3 days, or by phone if urgent. Do not wait for laboratory confirmation.
UKHSA 2024: hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, are excluded until 7 days after the onset of jaundice. The health protection team advises on the individual case and on return to work.

professional.t: Offer HIV testing as routine and obtain verbal consent (NICE NG60; BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020). Explain window periods rather than giving false reassurance.

His sexual history is confidential (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Partner notification is best done through the sexual health clinic, with his agreement. Disclosure without consent is for serious risk of harm only and would not arise from these facts alone.

community.t: Local sexual health clinic for confidential partner testing and notification; UKHSA health protection team for contact vaccination; travel health advice, including hepatitis A vaccination, before future trips.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, rising INR or deepening jaundice: acute liver failure, same-day hospital
Fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area: same-day malaria films
Jaundice aged 40 and over without an infective cause: suspected pancreatic cancer pathway (not applicable at 26)
psychosocial: Chef and food handler: exclusion, income and fit note
Two-year relationship and guilt about new partners on the trip
Alcohol use and self-medication with paracetamol
ice: Idea: “A bug I picked up from the food travelling.”
Concern: hepatitis B, C or HIV caught through sex or the tattoo, and having to tell or having infected his girlfriend
Expectation: a return-to-work date and a tablet to speed recovery

playbook.diagnosis: Acute hepatitis (ALT 1840, bilirubin 96, normal INR) in a returning traveller: most likely acute viral hepatitis A or E, with acute hepatitis B and other blood-borne infection to exclude given unprotected sex and an unsterile tattoo. No features of acute liver failure today.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your liver is inflamed, which is why you’ve gone yellow. The most likely cause is a virus from food or water that usually clears on its own in a few weeks. Because of the other things you told me, we’ll test for the viruses that spread through sex and blood too, so you know for certain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping this is a food bug because the other possibility means talking to your girlfriend. Let’s find out properly, and whatever it is, there’s a plan.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and written exclusion to protect his income and job; support to plan disclosure in his own time; sexual health clinic for confidential partner testing.
sharedPlan: Hepatitis A, B, C and E serology, HIV with consent, repeat LFTs and INR; repeat HIV and hepatitis C after the window period (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020)
Notify on suspicion; no food handling until cleared, at least 7 days from jaundice onset (UKHSA 2024); contacts assessed for vaccine
No alcohol, paracetamol at standard doses only, no herbal remedies; condoms or no sex until results
safetyNet: A&E or 999 for confusion, drowsiness, bleeding, persistent vomiting or deepening jaundice
GP phones with results; repeat LFTs and INR booked; review at each result

pitfalls.intro: The diagnosis here is easy. The station is failed on what surrounds it: a risk history that never goes beyond food, a chef sent back to the kitchen, and a frightened young man left alone with the question he came to ask.

items.fail: Taking only a food and water history and accepting ‘travel bug’.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Sexual and tattoo exposure change the test panel and the partner plan.
items.fix: Normalise it: “I ask everyone the same questions, no judgement: new partners, tattoos or piercings, injections or procedures?”

items.fail: Telling a chef he can go back to work when he feels better.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” UKHSA 2024 excludes hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, until 7 days after jaundice onset, and notification is a statutory duty.
items.fix: State the exclusion, notify on suspicion, and give a fit note so the plan is workable.

items.fail: Telling him a clear HIV test today means he is fine.
items.why: False reassurance: a fourth-generation test excludes HIV only from 45 days after exposure (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020).
items.fix: “Some tests take weeks to turn positive, so we’ll repeat them later to be certain.”

items.fail: Reacting to the disclosure with a lecture about condoms or fidelity.
items.why: Judgemental responses are a recurring Relating fail and shut down further disclosure.
items.fix: Thank him, then move to what it means for his tests and his partner.

items.fail: Telling him he must inform his girlfriend today.
items.why: Takes control away from the patient; he disengages from testing.
items.fix: Protect her in the meantime (condoms or no sex, clinic testing) and offer help planning the conversation when he is ready.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if you get worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting misses the features of acute liver failure.
items.fix: Name confusion, drowsiness, bleeding, vomiting and deepening jaundice, and give dated results and repeat testing.

SCA_MODELS.text: A couple of weeks ago I had a temperature, felt sick and achy. I thought it was flu. Then four days ago the yellow started, the wee went dark and my poo went pale. Sore just under my right ribs.
Any confusion or drowsiness, bruising or bleeding from your gums, or vomiting so much you can’t keep fluids down? And has the fever come back at all?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for acute liver failure and for fever that would need malaria films

SCA_MODELS.text: No, none of that. No fever since. Just tired and off my food.
Good. Tell me about the food and water out there.
SCA_MODELS.why: Covers the faeco-oral route for hepatitis A and E

SCA_MODELS.text: Street food every day, salads, ice in drinks, sometimes tap water. It’s a bug from the food, right?

That’s the most likely route. Everyone I see with this gets the same full set of questions, with no judgement, because the answer changes which tests we do. On the trip, any new sexual partners, any tattoos or piercings, and any injections, medical or dental treatment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Normalises the question and covers the blood-borne and sexual routes

SCA_MODELS.text: …Yeah. A couple of girls, no condoms. And I got a tattoo in a hostel town. I wasn’t thinking.
Thank you for telling me. That is genuinely useful, and it isn’t something to feel ashamed about here. Any drugs by injection, and any alcohol or medicines recently, including paracetamol?
SCA_MODELS.why: Rewards the disclosure without moralising and completes the toxin history

SCA_MODELS.text: Never injected anything. A few beers out there, nothing since I got ill. Couple of paracetamol for the ache.
You went quiet before you told me about the trip. I wonder whether the thing keeping you awake isn’t the yellow at all.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the cue behind the pause and invites the hidden concern

SCA_MODELS.text: My girlfriend. We’ve been together two years. That trip was meant to be the lads’ thing before we settle down. If this is hepatitis B or HIV, I have to tell her. And what if I’ve already given it to her?
That’s a lot to have been carrying on your own. So the real hope today is to find out whether this is a food bug or something caught through sex, and whether she’s at risk?
SCA_MODELS.why: Reflects the concern and confirms the real expectation

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. That’s it.

Here’s what I think. Your liver is inflamed, which is why you’re yellow. The pattern in your blood test, after a month of street food, most likely fits hepatitis A or E, which come from food and water. They usually settle by themselves over a few weeks, and your clotting test is normal, which tells me the liver is still doing its main jobs.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains acute hepatocellular hepatitis in plain words, with its likely cause

SCA_MODELS.text: So it probably is the food?

Probably, but I won’t guess. I’d like one blood sample today that checks for hepatitis A, B, C and E, and, with your agreement, HIV. I’ll repeat the liver and clotting tests too. I should be honest that HIV and hepatitis C can take several weeks to show, so if the first results are clear we may repeat them later to be sure.
SCA_MODELS.why: Full viral and blood-borne panel with consent, and honest testing windows

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, test for all of it. I’d rather know.

Now the part you didn’t expect. Hepatitis from food spreads through food. As a chef, you mustn’t work in the kitchen until you’re cleared: at least a week from when the yellow started, and the public health team advises on your return. I have a legal duty to notify them, and they will also check whether people close to you need a vaccine.
SCA_MODELS.why: States the food-handler exclusion and the statutory notification

SCA_MODELS.text: A week off? I can’t afford that.

I know it hits your wages. I’ll give you a fit note, and the public health team can confirm the exclusion in writing for your employer, which also protects your job. Is money going to be a real problem?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the financial impact and offers practical help

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll manage if I get sick pay. The boss is alright.

About your girlfriend: condoms, or no sex, until your results are back. If she has been close to you since you got home, the public health team may offer her a hepatitis A vaccine, and the sexual health clinic can test her confidentially. When and how you tell her is your decision, and I’m happy to help you plan it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Protects the partner and supports disclosure without taking control from him

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I think I do need to tell her. Just not before I know what it is.

That’s a reasonable plan. While you recover: no alcohol at all, eat what you can, drink plenty, and paracetamol only at normal doses. No herbal remedies. And there isn’t a tablet to speed up this kind of hepatitis; rest is the treatment.
SCA_MODELS.why: Hepatotoxin advice and an honest answer to his tablet question

SCA_MODELS.text: Please go straight to A&E, or call 999 if you can’t get there, if you become confused or very sleepy, bruise or bleed easily, can’t keep fluids down, or go more yellow. I’ll ring you with the results in a few days, and we’ll book a repeat test for later.
SCA_MODELS.why: Named acute liver failure red flags and dated follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
So I know I’ve explained it properly, what will you tell your boss tomorrow?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back on the point he most needs to act on

SCA_MODELS.text: That I’ve got hepatitis, probably from food, and I can’t cook until public health clears me. And I’ll get a sick note.
Exactly. You did the right thing by telling me everything today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes warmly and reinforces the disclosure

SCA_STEM.name: Jay Mistry
SCA_STEM.recent: Returned 12 days ago from a month backpacking in India and South-East Asia. E-consult this week: yellow eyes for 4 days, dark urine, pale stools. Bloods today: ALT 1840 U/L, AST 1100 U/L, bilirubin 96 µmol/L, ALP mildly raised, INR normal. No viral serology on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss jaundice and his blood results.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UKHSA Public health control and management of hepatitis A (2024) · UKHSA Green Book ch.17 (2024) · Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 · NICE NG60 · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA HIV testing guidelines (2020) · BSG abnormal liver blood tests guideline (2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Jaundice with ALT in the thousands in a returning traveller is acute viral hepatitis until proven otherwise, most often A or E. Check synthetic function, test the full viral and blood-borne panel with consent, notify on suspicion, and exclude a food handler from work.

points.t: Transaminases in the thousands with a modest ALP rise is a hepatocellular picture: viral, drug or toxin, ischaemic or autoimmune hepatitis. A normal INR is reassuring about synthetic function today; it must be repeated because it is the earliest marker of liver failure. BSG 2018: refer urgently if there is synthetic failure or marked derangement.

Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and core IgM, hepatitis C antibody (with RNA if positive), hepatitis E, and an HIV test with consent (NICE NG60). BSG 2018 advises HEV testing when A, B and C are negative; test it up front in a returning traveller. Malaria films if there has been any fever after travel to an endemic area.

BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020: a fourth-generation HIV test excludes infection only from 45 days after the last exposure, so an early negative needs repeating. Hepatitis C antibody can take weeks to months to appear; RNA testing detects it earlier. Tell him plainly that one clear set of results may not be the last word.

Acute infectious hepatitis is notifiable on clinical suspicion (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010): written notice to the proper officer within 3 days, by phone if urgent. UKHSA 2024: exclude hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, until 7 days after the onset of jaundice; the health protection team advises on return and on hepatitis E.

Hepatitis A is infectious from about 2 weeks before symptoms to 1 week after jaundice. UKHSA 2024: hepatitis A vaccine within 14 days of exposure for healthy close contacts aged 1 and over; the health protection team arranges it, adding immunoglobulin for higher-risk contacts. Household and sexual contacts, including his girlfriend, need assessing.

Confusion, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, a rising INR or deepening jaundice mean same-day hospital assessment. Avoid alcohol; paracetamol at standard doses only, avoiding large doses (BNF). For contrast: NICE suspected-cancer guidance refers people aged 40 and over with jaundice on a suspected pancreatic cancer pathway, which does not apply to Jay at 26.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question about how he feels; heard the work and ‘quick fix’ questions without letting them set the agenda.
Chef and food handler, income worries, relationship of two years, alcohol use.
Picked up the pause about the trip and the over-firm ‘travel bug’ and opened the sexual and tattoo history safely.
Idea (food bug), concern (blood-borne infection and his girlfriend), expectation (return-to-work date and a tablet).
Hepatitis A, B, C and E serology; HIV with consent; repeat LFTs and INR; malaria films if febrile; repeat tests after the window period.
Hepatitis A or E vs acute hepatitis B vs drug or toxin injury; tested with food, sexual, tattoo, injecting and medication history.
Asked about confusion, drowsiness, bleeding and vomiting; normal INR noted and repeated; same-day admission criteria known.
Acute viral hepatitis, most likely A or E, explained in plain words with the cause still to confirm.
Notification on suspicion; food-handler exclusion for at least 7 days from jaundice onset per UKHSA; fit note; no alcohol, standard paracetamol doses.
Partner protection and testing, contact vaccination via the health protection team, sexual health signposting.
Liver failure red flags named; results phoned; repeat HIV and hepatitis C testing timed after the window period.

social.t: A chef paid by the shift faces lost income from exclusion. Offer a fit note and written confirmation of exclusion from the health protection team; he is likely to be eligible for Statutory Sick Pay.
Guilt about sex outside the relationship drives both the concealment and the anxiety. Support disclosure at his pace while making sure his partner is protected and can be tested.

legal.t: Acute infectious hepatitis is notifiable on clinical suspicion under the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010: written notice to the proper officer within 3 days, or by phone if urgent. Do not wait for laboratory confirmation.
UKHSA 2024: hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, are excluded until 7 days after the onset of jaundice. The health protection team advises on the individual case and on return to work.

professional.t: Offer HIV testing as routine and obtain verbal consent (NICE NG60; BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020). Explain window periods rather than giving false reassurance.

His sexual history is confidential (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Partner notification is best done through the sexual health clinic, with his agreement. Disclosure without consent is for serious risk of harm only and would not arise from these facts alone.

community.t: Local sexual health clinic for confidential partner testing and notification; UKHSA health protection team for contact vaccination; travel health advice, including hepatitis A vaccination, before future trips.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, rising INR or deepening jaundice: acute liver failure, same-day hospital
Fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area: same-day malaria films
Jaundice aged 40 and over without an infective cause: suspected pancreatic cancer pathway (not applicable at 26)
psychosocial: Chef and food handler: exclusion, income and fit note
Two-year relationship and guilt about new partners on the trip
Alcohol use and self-medication with paracetamol
ice: Idea: “A bug I picked up from the food travelling.”
Concern: hepatitis B, C or HIV caught through sex or the tattoo, and having to tell or having infected his girlfriend
Expectation: a return-to-work date and a tablet to speed recovery

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Acute hepatitis (ALT 1840, bilirubin 96, normal INR) in a returning traveller: most likely acute viral hepatitis A or E, with acute hepatitis B and other blood-borne infection to exclude given unprotected sex and an unsterile tattoo. No features of acute liver failure today.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your liver is inflamed, which is why you’ve gone yellow. The most likely cause is a virus from food or water that usually clears on its own in a few weeks. Because of the other things you told me, we’ll test for the viruses that spread through sex and blood too, so you know for certain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been hoping this is a food bug because the other possibility means talking to your girlfriend. Let’s find out properly, and whatever it is, there’s a plan.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and written exclusion to protect his income and job; support to plan disclosure in his own time; sexual health clinic for confidential partner testing.
sharedPlan: Hepatitis A, B, C and E serology, HIV with consent, repeat LFTs and INR; repeat HIV and hepatitis C after the window period (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020)
Notify on suspicion; no food handling until cleared, at least 7 days from jaundice onset (UKHSA 2024); contacts assessed for vaccine
No alcohol, paracetamol at standard doses only, no herbal remedies; condoms or no sex until results
safetyNet: A&E or 999 for confusion, drowsiness, bleeding, persistent vomiting or deepening jaundice
GP phones with results; repeat LFTs and INR booked; review at each result

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The diagnosis here is easy. The station is failed on what surrounds it: a risk history that never goes beyond food, a chef sent back to the kitchen, and a frightened young man left alone with the question he came to ask.

items.fail: Taking only a food and water history and accepting ‘travel bug’.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Sexual and tattoo exposure change the test panel and the partner plan.
items.fix: Normalise it: “I ask everyone the same questions, no judgement: new partners, tattoos or piercings, injections or procedures?”

items.fail: Telling a chef he can go back to work when he feels better.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” UKHSA 2024 excludes hepatitis A cases, including food handlers, until 7 days after jaundice onset, and notification is a statutory duty.
items.fix: State the exclusion, notify on suspicion, and give a fit note so the plan is workable.

items.fail: Telling him a clear HIV test today means he is fine.
items.why: False reassurance: a fourth-generation test excludes HIV only from 45 days after exposure (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020).
items.fix: “Some tests take weeks to turn positive, so we’ll repeat them later to be certain.”

items.fail: Reacting to the disclosure with a lecture about condoms or fidelity.
items.why: Judgemental responses are a recurring Relating fail and shut down further disclosure.
items.fix: Thank him, then move to what it means for his tests and his partner.

items.fail: Telling him he must inform his girlfriend today.
items.why: Takes control away from the patient; he disengages from testing.
items.fix: Protect her in the meantime (condoms or no sex, clinic testing) and offer help planning the conversation when he is ready.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if you get worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting misses the features of acute liver failure.
items.fix: Name confusion, drowsiness, bleeding, vomiting and deepening jaundice, and give dated results and repeat testing.
